lead: Bitcoin payments are public, but names are not attached. Each address is a pseudonym. Because every transaction stays on the ledger, address reuse, co-spent inputs and data from KYC exchanges can join those pseudonyms into one identity. This chapter explains that linkage, then the tools that reduce it: mixers, CoinJoin, confidential amounts, ring signatures and shielded pools. It matters to users who want financial privacy, to exchanges that must follow rules, and to investigators who trace stolen coins.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for UTXOs and Chapter 4.5 for how transactions spread.

blocks.text: Bitcoin is pseudonymous. An address is a pseudonym: a string that stands in for a key owner. The blockchain records the address, amount and time of every payment. It does not record a name, a phone number or a PAN. Anyone can read the ledger. This is public auditability, not privacy.

Two things reduce privacy: address reuse and co-spending. Address reuse means receiving many payments at one address, so one public label collects your history. Co-spending is stronger. A transaction spends unspent outputs (UTXOs, from Chapter 4.2). If one transaction spends outputs from A1 and A2, the common-input-ownership heuristic infers that one wallet controls both keys. A valid spend needs a signature for every input, so the builder had both private keys. Exchanges, wallets and chain-analysis firms use this heuristic to cluster addresses.

Clustering puts addresses into one guessed owner. Taint follows a coin's history: if a coin passed through a flagged address, later holders may be treated as suspicious. Taint is a risk score, not proof. A mixer adds hops; it does not erase history.

sections.h3: Chain analysis and the KYC link

blocks.text: Chain analysis reads public ledger data to guess ownership and flow. It uses several signals:

items: change outputs: one output pays the recipient, the remainder returns to the sender's new change address;
timing and amounts: a withdrawal at 10:02 and a deposit at 10:05 may be the same coins;
off-chain data: invoices, forum posts, shipping records, leaked databases.

blocks.text: The strongest link is a KYC exchange. KYC means Know Your Customer: the exchange verifies a legal name, address and ID. When the customer withdraws bitcoin, the exchange records the withdrawal address. A lawful request can then connect that address to a verified person. Clustering spreads the label to co-spent addresses.

A single transaction that spends A1 and A2 lets the heuristic link them, and if the exchange knows the name behind one input, that name spreads to the rest of the cluster. One KYC withdrawal can expose a cluster.

Mixers break the direct link. A custodial mixer takes coins, pools them, and pays out from a different address, minus a fee. It relies on trust: the operator can steal or keep records. CoinJoin is trustless in the sense that no operator holds the coins: several users build one transaction with many inputs and many equal-value outputs. Many implementations use a coordinator that cannot steal funds but may learn the input-output mapping unless the round is blinded. An outside observer sees many possible owners for each output. CoinJoin does not hide amounts, and poor timing or unusual amounts can still leak links.

Confidential transactions hide the amount, not the addresses. They use cryptographic commitments so the network can check that inputs equal outputs without seeing values. Monero uses ring signatures and RingCT: a real input hides among decoys, and amounts are hidden by commitments. Zcash has shielded pools that hide sender, receiver and amount using zero-knowledge proofs, as Chapter 4.7 introduces. Transparent Zcash transactions behave like Bitcoin.

Privacy coins and mixers face legal scrutiny. Many exchanges delist coins with strong anonymity, and some jurisdictions require reporting. Privacy is legal in many places; using it to evade tax or launder money is not. A mixer does not make coins clean.

figure.caption: A KYC exchange funds A1. A1 and A2 are spent together in D, so the common-input heuristic links them to one owner. D pays 1.09 BTC to E; the 0.01 BTC difference is the fee.

spec.aria: A directed graph: a KYC exchange funds address A1 with 0.8 BTC; A1 and A2 co-spend 0.8 and 0.3 BTC into transaction D; D pays 1.09 BTC to E; the co-spend links A1 and A2 to one owner.

examples.question: Address A1 receives 0.8 BTC from a KYC exchange. A2 holds 0.3 BTC. One transaction spends both inputs and pays 1.09 BTC to E, with a 0.01 BTC fee. What does the common-input heuristic infer, and what does the exchange know?
steps: List the inputs: A1 has 0.8 BTC and A2 has 0.3 BTC.
Add the output and fee: 1.09 + 0.01 = 1.1 BTC. Inputs equal outputs plus fee, so the transaction is balanced.
Apply the common-input heuristic: one transaction spends A1 and A2, so one wallet likely controls both keys.
The exchange has a KYC record for the withdrawal to A1. By clustering, it can attach that verified name to A2. It may also see E as the recipient of 1.09 BTC.
examples.answer: The heuristic links A1 and A2 to one owner, and the exchange can attach its KYC name for A1 to A2; the transaction moves 1.09 BTC to E with a 0.01 BTC fee.
examples.check:
in1 = 0.8
in2 = 0.3
out = 1.09
fee = 0.01
total_in = in1 + in2
assert abs((out + fee) - total_in) < 1e-12
print(total_in)
print(out)
print(fee)

traps: Saying Bitcoin is anonymous. Every payment is public and permanent; addresses are pseudonyms, not names.
Treating co-spending as proof. It is a heuristic; exchange co-spending can create false clusters.
Saying a mixer makes coins clean. It adds a hop; taint remains and chain analysis may cross it.
Confusing CoinJoin with confidential transactions. CoinJoin hides links; confidential transactions hide amounts.
Thinking KYC links only deposits. The exchange also records withdrawal addresses, which seed clustering.

quiz.a: A pseudonym is an address that stands for a key owner; the ledger shows the address, not the legal name.

quiz.q: Why does co-spending two inputs suggest one owner?
quiz.a: A valid transaction needs a signature for each input, so the builder likely held both private keys.

quiz.q: Inputs are 0.5 BTC and 0.2 BTC; one output is 0.69 BTC. What is the fee, and what does the common-input heuristic infer?
quiz.a: Inputs total 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7 BTC. Output plus fee must be 0.7 BTC, so fee = 0.7 - 0.69 = 0.01 BTC. The heuristic links the two input addresses to one likely owner.

quiz.q: An exchange sweeps deposits from many customers' addresses into one transaction. How can this mislead clustering?
quiz.a: The common-input heuristic may label all those customers as one owner, creating a false cluster; an analyst must treat the link as probabilistic.

quiz.q: What does KYC mean, and why is an exchange a strong link to a name?
quiz.a: Know Your Customer; the exchange verifies identity and records withdrawal addresses, so a lawful request can tie a name to an address.

quiz.q: How is CoinJoin different from confidential transactions?
quiz.a: CoinJoin hides which inputs own which outputs by joint spending. Confidential transactions hide the amounts using commitments, not the addresses.

quiz.q: Compare the trust model of a custodial mixer and CoinJoin.
quiz.a: A custodial mixer trusts an operator who can steal or keep records. CoinJoin is built by users in one transaction, so no operator holds the coins, though analysis can still link.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern wallets use avoid-reuse and coin control to reduce clustering. Researchers study how exchange co-spending creates false clusters. Privacy engineering now includes payment channels and stealth addresses. Regulators debate travel-rule data sharing for virtual assets. Search for common-input ownership heuristic, CoinJoin, ring confidential transactions and shielded pools.
